q: A factory's sales for a year are Rs 60,00,000. Its bought-in materials cost Rs 22,00,000 and bought-in services cost Rs 8,00,000. Its gross value added for the year is:
The net value added of an enterprise differs from its gross value added in that the net value added is arrived at after deducting:

options.A: Wages and salaries paid to employees
options.B: Taxes paid to the government
options.C: Interest paid to lenders
options.D: Depreciation, representing the value of fixed assets consumed in creating the value added

q: In a Value Added Statement, wages and salaries are shown:

options.A: As an expense deducted from sales in arriving at the value added
options.B: Only in a footnote, as they do not form part of the statement
options.C: As a share of the value added distributed to the employees who helped to create it, and not as a charge in creating it
options.D: As an amount payable to the government

q: Under the replacement cost approach to human resource accounting, the value placed on the human resources of an organisation includes the cost that would be incurred in:

options.A: Paying retrenchment compensation to all employees
options.B: Recruiting, hiring and training a replacement employee of equivalent ability and experience
options.C: Settling the provident fund dues of retiring employees
options.D: Providing residential accommodation to employees

q: Human resources do not find a place as an asset in the conventional balance sheet mainly because:

options.A: The enterprise does not own its employees and cannot control their services as it controls a physical asset, and there is no generally accepted and reliable basis for measuring their value in money
options.B: Employees contribute nothing to the earnings of an enterprise
options.C: The Companies Act requires all assets to be physical in nature
options.D: The wages paid to employees are too small to be recorded

q: The Current Cost Accounting (CCA) method of inflation accounting differs from the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method in the nature of the capital it seeks to maintain, in that CCA aims at maintaining:

options.A: Only the cash balance of the enterprise
options.B: Capital in terms of a general price index
options.C: The nominal money amount of the original investment
options.D: The operating capability of the enterprise, that is, its physical productive capacity

q: An asset was purchased for Rs 3,60,000 when the general price index stood at 120. At the balance sheet date the index stands at 200. Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method, the restated value of the asset is:

At the beginning of a year, an enterprise holds cash and debtors of Rs 8,00,000 and has monetary liabilities of Rs 5,00,000. During the year the general price level rises by 10 per cent, the monetary position remaining unchanged in money terms throughout. Under CPP accounting, the enterprise records:

options.A: A purchasing power gain of Rs 30,000
options.B: A purchasing power loss of Rs 30,000
options.C: A purchasing power loss of Rs 80,000
options.D: No purchasing power gain or loss

q: In Current Cost Accounting (CCA), the 'gearing adjustment' is made in order to:

options.A: Credit back to profit the proportion of the other current-cost adjustments that is borne by the providers of loan finance rather than by the shareholders, in proportion to the gearing of the enterprise
options.B: Increase the depreciation charge on fixed assets
options.C: Restate the stock for the rise in its replacement cost
options.D: Provide for the repayment of debentures at maturity

q: Under the quantitative thresholds applied in segment reporting, a segment is reportable if, among other tests, its revenue amounts to at least the following proportion of the combined revenue of all segments:

options.A: 5 per cent
options.B: 25 per cent
options.C: 10 per cent
options.D: 50 per cent

q: The revenue of a segment of an enterprise is Rs 18,00,000 and the combined revenue of all its segments is Rs 1,50,00,000. Judged by the revenue test for reportable segments, the segment:

options.A: Does not qualify, its revenue being only 8 per cent of the combined revenue
options.B: Qualifies only if its assets also exceed 50 per cent of the total assets
options.C: Qualifies as reportable, its revenue being 12 per cent of the combined revenue, above the 10 per cent threshold
options.D: Cannot be judged, as the test is based on profit alone

q: Under Ind AS 108, operating segments are identified on the 'management approach', which means that segments are based on:

options.A: The geographical areas in which the enterprise happens to own property
options.B: The components about which internal reports are regularly prepared and reviewed by the chief operating decision maker for allocating resources and assessing performance
options.C: The product lines named in the memorandum of association of the company
options.D: A uniform list of segments prescribed for all enterprises

q: A zonal railway shows a noticeably better Operating Ratio for a year mainly because essential maintenance of track and rolling stock was deferred during that year. The sound interpretation of the improved ratio is that:

options.A: The improvement is only apparent, having been bought at the cost of asset condition and of heavier expenditure in later years, and does not by itself evidence a genuine gain in efficiency
options.B: The zone has permanently reduced its cost of maintenance
options.C: Deferred maintenance has no effect on the Operating Ratio
options.D: The Operating Ratio should be recomputed after adding back the capital expenditure of the year

q: A railway records an Operating Ratio below 100 for a year. This fact alone does not establish that the railway will have a surplus available after meeting its dividend obligation to General Revenues, because:

options.A: The Operating Ratio is computed only for passenger services
options.B: Gross traffic receipts exclude all coaching earnings
options.C: The dividend is itself a part of the gross working expenses
options.D: The Operating Ratio is worked out from gross working expenses alone and takes no account of the dividend payable on the capital-at-charge, which is met out of the net revenue

q: The Operating Ratio of one zonal railway is higher than that of another for the same year. Before ranking the two zones by efficiency on this evidence alone, an analyst should:

options.A: Treat the higher-ratio zone as inefficient without further enquiry
options.B: Compare only the gross earnings of the two zones
options.C: Allow for structural differences between the zones, such as terrain, the mix of passenger and freight traffic and the average lead, and read the ratio together with other indicators such as unit costs
options.D: Recompute both ratios after excluding all staff costs

q: A works manager supports buying a part from outside by comparing the supplier's price with the full factory cost of the part, which includes a share of the general factory rent apportioned to his shop. The rent will be paid in full whether the part is made or bought. For the make-or-buy comparison, the apportioned rent should be:

options.A: Added to the supplier's price
options.B: Excluded, because it is a common cost unaffected by the decision
options.C: Treated as a saving expected from buying
options.D: Spread over the remaining products and added to the cost of making

q: A part is made in 10,000 units a year. Its variable cost of making is Rs 45 per unit (material Rs 22, labour Rs 14, variable overhead Rs 9), and supervision costing Rs 30,000 a year would be given up entirely if the part were bought. An outside supplier quotes Rs 52 per unit. On relevant costs, the firm should:

options.A: Buy, saving Rs 40,000 a year
options.B: Buy, saving Rs 70,000 a year
options.C: Make, saving Rs 40,000 a year
options.D: Make, saving Rs 70,000 a year

q: Making a gear in-house costs a variable Rs 58 per unit. A vendor offers the same gear at Rs 68 per unit. If the gear is bought, the bench so freed can be turned to other work yielding a contribution of Rs 7 per gear-equivalent. The correct comparison and decision are:

options.A: Compare Rs 58 with Rs 68 and buy
options.B: Compare Rs 58 with Rs 61 and make
options.C: Compare Rs 65 with Rs 68 and buy
options.D: Compare Rs 58 with Rs 75 and make

q: On pure relevant-cost figures, buying a component works out marginally cheaper than making it. Before acting on the figures alone, management should also weigh:

options.A: The book value of the machine presently used for the component
options.B: The depreciation already charged on that machine in past years
options.C: The reliability of the outside supply and the control retained over quality and delivery schedules
options.D: The share of head-office expenses absorbed by the component last year

q: Kiln time is the scarce resource of a pottery unit making several wares. So long as kiln time remains the binding constraint, the ware to be pushed is the one showing the highest:

options.A: Selling price per piece
options.B: Contribution per piece
options.C: Net profit per piece after absorbing all overheads
options.D: Contribution per kiln-hour

q: Three articles share one bottleneck process. Article P yields a contribution of Rs 90 per unit and takes 3 bottleneck hours; Article Q yields Rs 110 per unit and takes 5 bottleneck hours; Article R yields Rs 64 per unit and takes 2 bottleneck hours. The order of production priority is:

options.A: R first, then P, then Q
options.B: Q first, then P, then R
options.C: P first, then R, then Q
options.D: Q first, then R, then P

q: A plant has 12,000 kg of a scarce alloy. Product X earns a contribution of Rs 50 per unit and consumes 5 kg per unit; its maximum demand is 1,000 units. Product Y earns Rs 36 per unit and consumes 4 kg per unit, with unlimited demand. After X is produced to its full demand, the units of Y that can be produced are:

options.A: 1,400 units
options.B: 3,000 units
options.C: 2,000 units
options.D: 1,750 units

q: After a product mix has been optimised on the principal key factor and the full programme is drawn up, a second resource is found to fall short of what the programme needs. In such a case, the correct course is to:

options.A: Retain the programme, since only the principal key factor matters
options.B: Rank the products by contribution per unit and cut the lowest-ranked product
options.C: Raise the selling prices until the demand for the second resource falls
options.D: Revise the programme treating the second resource as a further constraint, ranking by contribution per unit of the newly binding factor

q: Trade is slack and a section of a plant is working well below capacity. Short of a permanent closure decision, the section deserves to be kept running for the time being so long as:

options.A: Its receipts cover its full cost including apportioned head-office charges
options.B: The contribution it earns exceeds the fixed costs that would actually be saved by stopping it
options.C: It has earned a profit in at least one of the last three years
options.D: Its machinery has not yet been fully depreciated

q: The fixed costs of a works are Rs 3,60,000 a year, of which Rs 1,20,000 would go on being incurred even if the works were shut down for the whole year. The contribution is Rs 40 per unit. The shutdown point, in units of output, is:

options.A: 6,000 units
options.B: 3,000 units
options.C: 9,000 units
options.D: 12,000 units

q: At the expected volume of 4,000 units, a plant would earn a contribution of Rs 55 per unit. Its fixed costs are Rs 3,50,000, of which Rs 2,60,000 are avoidable on shutdown and Rs 90,000 would continue during shutdown. Comparing the two courses, the plant should:

options.A: Continue, because shutdown would lose Rs 1,30,000 against a loss of Rs 90,000 on continuing
options.B: Continue, because the contribution covers the whole of the unavoidable costs
options.C: Shut down, because shutdown would lose Rs 90,000 against a loss of Rs 1,30,000 on continuing
options.D: Shut down, because the avoidable fixed costs exceed the total fixed costs saved by continuing

q: In working out the loss that a temporary shutdown would still leave behind, which of the following items properly belongs to that reckoning?

options.A: The original cost of the plant lying idle
options.B: Standing charges that go on during the closure, such as watch and ward, insurance and the cost of mothballing and restarting
options.C: The profit the plant might have earned at full capacity
options.D: Depreciation already provided in earlier years

q: Idle benches and idle machine time are available in a factory. A one-off bulk enquiry is being priced. The floor below which the quoted price must not fall, if the order is to add anything to profit, is set by:

options.A: The full cost per unit at normal capacity, including absorbed fixed overheads
options.B: The average cost per unit of the previous year
options.C: The variable cost per unit plus any extra fixed outlay the order itself brings with it, spread over the order quantity
options.D: The price charged to the firm's regular dealers

q: Lying within spare capacity, a factory is offered a single bulk order for 8,000 units at Rs 48 per unit. The variable cost is Rs 42 per unit. Taking the order calls for a special jig costing Rs 24,000, of no later use. The order should be:

options.A: Refused, because the jig wipes out half the price margin
options.B: Accepted, because it adds Rs 24,000 to profit after meeting the jig cost
options.C: Refused, because Rs 48 is below the normal list price of the article
options.D: Accepted only if the buyer also bears the jig cost separately

q: Regular sales of an article are made at Rs 120 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 70 per unit. A special order for 3,000 units at Rs 95 per unit can be taken only by giving up 1,000 units of regular sales, capacity being fully engaged otherwise. Taking the order would:

options.A: Reduce profit by Rs 25,000
options.B: Add Rs 75,000 to profit
options.C: Add Rs 25,000 to profit, after allowing for the regular contribution forgone
options.D: Leave profit unchanged

q: A one-time order priced well below the list price but above variable cost is commercially attractive while benches lie idle. A standing caution before quoting such a price to the buyer is that:

options.A: The low price may become known and be demanded as a precedent by regular customers, or may disturb the normal market for the product
options.B: The order will necessarily push the firm below its break-even point
options.C: Variable cost per unit rises whenever output rises
options.D: Fixed costs must be re-absorbed on the order quantity before it is quoted

q: A joint product emerging at the split-off point can either be sold as it stands or carried through a further process. The share of the joint costs incurred up to the split-off point, apportioned to this product, is for the sell-or-process-further choice:

options.A: To be added to the further-processing cost
options.B: To be deducted from the price obtainable at split-off
options.C: To be recovered in full before any further processing is allowed
options.D: Irrelevant, because it has already been incurred whichever course is taken; only the extra revenue and the extra processing cost count

q: A product can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 90 per unit. By spending Rs 28 per unit on a further process, it can be sold instead for Rs 130 per unit. The firm should:

options.A: Process further, gaining Rs 12 per unit over selling at split-off
options.B: Sell at split-off, because the further process costs Rs 28 per unit
options.C: Process further, gaining Rs 40 per unit
options.D: Sell at split-off, because the joint cost is recovered only at that stage

q: A batch of an intermediate product can be sold as it is for Rs 2,00,000. Carrying it through a finishing process costing Rs 65,000 would let the batch be sold for Rs 2,90,000. The firm should:

options.A: Sell the batch as it is and save the finishing cost
options.B: Finish the batch only if the finishing cost falls below Rs 50,000
options.C: Sell the batch as it is, because the gain on finishing is less than the finishing cost
options.D: Finish the batch, gaining Rs 25,000 over selling it as it is

q: Judging whether a department of a store deserves to be closed, the figure that decides the matter is the department's segment margin, namely:

options.A: Its contribution less the fixed costs that would actually be avoided by closing it
options.B: Its sales less its variable costs alone
options.C: Its net profit after charging a full share of the store's common rent and management salaries
options.D: Its gross profit as shown in the departmental trading account

q: A section shows sales of Rs 5,00,000 and variable costs of Rs 3,20,000. Of its fixed costs, Rs 2,00,000 would cease if the section were closed, while Rs 60,000 of apportioned common costs would go on and fall on the other sections. Closing the section would change the firm's total profit by:

options.A: A fall of Rs 1,20,000
options.B: A fall of Rs 20,000
options.C: A rise of Rs 20,000
options.D: A rise of Rs 1,20,000

q: The accounts of a product line, after absorbing a share of the factory's common overheads, show a small loss, though its contribution comfortably exceeds every cost that would disappear with the line. Dropping the line on the strength of the reported loss would:

options.A: Save the whole of the loss shown in the accounts
options.B: Leave total profit unchanged, the common overheads being merely re-spread
options.C: Raise total profit by the amount of the common overheads absorbed
options.D: Reduce total profit, because the common overheads would continue while the line's net contribution towards them is lost

q: A house sells two lines in a steady sales proportion. A single break-even figure for the house as a whole is worked out by:

options.A: Averaging the separate break-even points of the two lines
options.B: Using a weighted average P/V ratio, the weights being the shares of the two lines in total sales, on the footing that the sales mix stays unchanged
options.C: Taking the P/V ratio of the line with the larger sales
options.D: Adding the fixed costs of the two lines and dividing by the higher P/V ratio

q: Line A has sales of Rs 6,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 40% and Line B has sales of Rs 4,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 20%. The sales mix is steady and the common fixed costs are Rs 2,56,000. The combined break-even sales of the house are:
Trading results show a wide margin of safety alongside a modest rate of profit on sales. Read together, the two figures indicate that:

options.A: The firm is operating close to its break-even point
options.B: Sales could fall a long way before losses begin, but each rupee of sales carries only a thin contribution after variable costs
options.C: The P/V ratio must be high
options.D: Fixed costs must be negligible

q: An undertaking sells Rs 25,00,000 worth of goods, its break-even sales being Rs 15,00,000 and its P/V ratio 30%. Its profit at the present level of sales is:
The margin of safety of a business, measured in sales value, is Rs 6,00,000 and its P/V ratio is 35%. The profit earned is:
A target is set in terms of the profit to be left after tax. To find the sales that will yield that target, the after-tax profit must first be:

options.A: Reduced by the tax payable on it
options.B: Treated as the profit before tax itself
options.C: Grossed up by dividing it by (1 minus the tax rate), so as to reach the profit before tax that the sales must produce
options.D: Increased by the fixed costs of the period

q: A company wishes to leave a profit after tax of Rs 1,50,000, the rate of tax being 20%. Its fixed costs are Rs 3,12,500 and its P/V ratio is 25%. The sales needed to meet the target are:

An article sells at Rs 160 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 100 per unit and fixed costs of Rs 4,20,000. The profit aimed at, after tax at 25%, is Rs 1,80,000. The units that must be sold to reach that aim are:

options.A: 10,000 units
options.B: 11,000 units
options.C: 9,400 units
options.D: 12,500 units

q: Two firms in the same trade earn the same operating profit at the present volume, but Firm H carries a much heavier burden of fixed costs, met by a higher contribution margin, than Firm L. A sharp fall in demand would:

options.A: Hit Firm H harder, because its profit depends on a high volume to absorb its fixed costs — the mark of high operating leverage
options.B: Hit both firms equally, their present profits being equal
options.C: Hit Firm L harder, because its contribution margin is thinner
options.D: Leave Firm H untouched, because a high contribution margin guarantees profit

q: Sales of a concern are Rs 18,00,000, variable costs Rs 10,80,000 and fixed costs Rs 4,80,000. The degree of operating leverage at this level of sales is:
The degree of operating leverage is measured as contribution divided by operating profit. Exactly at the break-even point, this measure:

options.A: Equals one
options.B: Equals zero
options.C: Equals the P/V ratio
options.D: Cannot be meaningfully stated, the operating profit in the denominator being zero

q: An article sells at Rs 250 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 150 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 7,00,000 and the plant can turn out 10,000 units a year. The break-even point, expressed as a percentage of the plant's capacity, is:

The fixed costs of a concern for a year are Rs 5,00,000, in which depreciation of Rs 1,00,000 is included. The P/V ratio is 50%. The cash break-even sales, at which the concern just meets its cash outgoings, are:
Management is weighing a proposal to replace a hand process by a machine process for one operation only, output remaining the same. The comparison that governs the choice is between:

options.A: The average cost per unit under the two processes at last year's output
options.B: The total costs of the two processes at the expected output — a differential cost comparison, in which costs common to both drop out
options.C: The sunk cost of the hand tools and the price of the machine
options.D: The fixed costs alone, variable costs being the same under both

q: A bottleneck machine is fully booked. Taking a rush job on it means turning away regular work. In pricing the rush job, the contribution that the displaced regular work would have earned is:

options.A: Ignored, because no cash outlay is involved
options.B: Treated as a fixed overhead of the period
options.C: Charged only if the regular customer complains
options.D: An opportunity cost to be counted among the costs of accepting the rush job

q: A supplier's quoted price for a fitting comes out below even the variable cost of producing the fitting in the firm's own shop. On cost grounds, and subject to quality and continuity of supply, the comparison:

options.A: Still favours making, because fixed costs are sunk
options.B: Favours buying, and any avoidable fixed costs of making that are also saved strengthen the case further
options.C: Is evenly balanced, the two costs being broadly equal
options.D: Favours making, because buying at such a price must involve a hidden charge

q: Demand for every article of a unit exceeds what its bottleneck process can handle, and one article must be curtailed. The article to curtail is the one with:

options.A: The highest selling price
options.B: The largest sales volume in units
options.C: The lowest contribution per unit of the bottleneck factor
options.D: The lowest variable cost per unit

q: Idle capacity is available for a single order of 4,000 units. The variable cost is Rs 55 per unit and the order would call for a special packing outlay of Rs 20,000 in all, with no regular sale displaced. The lowest price per unit at which the order just pays for itself is:

options.A: Rs 60 per unit
options.B: Rs 55 per unit
options.C: Rs 75 per unit
options.D: Rs 50 per unit

q: A business is trading only slightly above its break-even level, so that its margin of safety is thin. The practical significance of that position is that:

options.A: Its fixed costs are about to rise
options.B: Its P/V ratio is necessarily below 10%
options.C: It enjoys a comfortable cushion against falling demand
options.D: Even a small drop in sales would carry it into loss, so its profit position is highly exposed

q: Without any change in prices, costs or total fixed costs, buyers shift from Line M (P/V ratio 50%) towards Line N (P/V ratio 20%) in a two-line business. The combined break-even point of the business will:

options.A: Rise, because a larger share of sales now comes from the line carrying the thinner contribution rate
options.B: Fall, because total sales are unchanged
options.C: Remain exactly where it was
options.D: Become impossible to compute

q: A shutdown decision is distinguished from a discontinuance decision in that a shutdown:

options.A: Involves selling off the plant and machinery at once
options.B: Permanently withdraws the product from the firm's range
options.C: Is judged by comparing lifetime profits under the two courses
options.D: Suspends operations for a time while keeping the plant and organisation intact for a later restart, whereas discontinuance gives up the line for good

q: Pricing a special job would use up a lot of material lying in store for which the firm has no other use and no prospect of one. The material cost the firm Rs 30,000; it could be sold off as it stands for Rs 8,000. The relevant cost of the material for the job is:

options.C: Rs 8,000, being the receipt forgone by using the material instead of selling it
options.D: Nil, the material being already in store

q: A firm mechanises an operation, replacing paid hand labour with a leased machine. Variable cost per unit falls and fixed costs rise by the amount of the lease. At volumes well above break-even the change raises profit, but its standing effect on the firm's risk is that:

options.A: Risk falls at every level of output
options.B: The break-even point falls and operating leverage falls with it
options.C: Operating leverage rises, so that profits swing more widely with changes in volume and a downturn hurts more than before
options.D: Operating leverage is unaffected, since total cost at the present volume is unchanged

q: The standard mix for a batch requiring a total input of 200 kg is: Material A — 120 kg at Rs 30 per kg and Material B — 80 kg at Rs 45 per kg. For one such batch the actual mix used is A — 100 kg and B — 100 kg, the total input remaining 200 kg. The material mix variance for the batch is:

options.A: Rs 300 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 300 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 600 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 900 (Adverse)

q: A process is fed with 500 kg of input material at a standard price of Rs 20 per kg. The standard yield from such input is 80 per cent, but the actual output obtained is only 380 kg. The material yield variance is:

options.A: Rs 500 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 400 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 500 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 1,000 (Adverse)

q: For the actual output, the standard quantities are: Material X — 600 kg at Rs 10 per kg and Material Y — 400 kg at Rs 15 per kg. The actual total quantity consumed is 1,100 kg. The material sub-usage (revised usage) variance, that is, the part of the usage variance arising after the actual total quantity is re-expressed in standard proportions, is:

options.A: Rs 1,200 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 1,200 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 600 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 200 (Favourable)

q: In a further analysis of the material usage variance, the revised standard quantity of a material means:

options.A: The actual quantity of that material valued at the actual price
options.B: The standard quantity allowed for the actual output, before any adjustment for the total quantity actually used
options.C: The quantity of that material actually consumed, restated at the standard price
options.D: The actual total quantity of all materials consumed, apportioned among the materials in their standard mix proportions

q: The standard gang for a shift's work comprises 100 hours of skilled labour at Rs 100 per hour and 200 hours of semi-skilled labour at Rs 60 per hour, a total of 300 hours. In an actual shift of 300 hours, 120 hours are worked by skilled labour and 180 hours by semi-skilled labour. The labour gang composition variance is:

options.A: Rs 800 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 2,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 1,200 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 800 (Adverse)

q: In labour variance analysis, after the effect of a change in the composition of the gang has been separated, the efficiency variance that remains is known as the:

options.A: Labour rate variance
options.B: Labour sub-efficiency variance
options.C: Idle time variance
options.D: Labour yield variance

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time allowed is 2,000 hours at a standard rate of Rs 45 per hour. The workers are paid for 2,100 hours, of which 100 hours are lost as abnormal idle time. The idle time variance is:

options.A: Rs 4,500 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 2,250 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 4,500 (Adverse)
options.D: Nil

q: A factory engages cheaper, less experienced labour and reports a favourable labour rate variance together with an adverse labour efficiency variance in the same period. The most likely explanation connecting the two variances is that:

options.A: The lower grade of labour, though cheaper per hour, took longer to do the work, so that the saving in rate was offset by a loss in efficiency
options.B: The two variances are wholly unrelated and must have arisen in different departments
options.C: The efficiency variance must be a mistake, because cheaper labour always works faster
options.D: The rate variance should be transferred to the production department to cancel the efficiency variance

q: The actual variable overheads of a department are Rs 92,000. The actual hours worked are 4,600 and the standard variable overhead rate is Rs 18 per hour. The variable overhead expenditure variance is:

options.A: Rs 9,200 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 82,800 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 4,600 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 9,200 (Adverse)

q: The standard time for the actual output is 2,400 hours, but 2,600 hours are actually worked. The standard variable overhead rate is Rs 16 per hour. The variable overhead efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 3,200 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 3,200 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 1,600 (Adverse)
options.D: Nil

q: The fixed overhead expenditure variance of a period is best understood as the part of the fixed overhead cost variance which:

options.A: Compares the budgeted fixed overheads with the actual fixed overheads incurred, and so reflects changes in the spending on, or the prices of, fixed cost items rather than any change in the volume of output
options.B: Arises because the actual output differs from the budgeted output
options.C: Is caused by working a different number of days from the number budgeted
options.D: Measures the efficiency with which the actual hours were utilised

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a factory are Rs 3,60,000 for a budgeted output of 12,000 units. The actual output is 13,500 units. The fixed overhead volume variance is:

options.A: Rs 45,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 30,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 45,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 27,000 (Favourable)

q: The budgeted working hours of a factory are 10,000 and the actual hours worked are 9,200. The standard fixed overhead absorption rate is Rs 24 per hour. The fixed overhead capacity variance is:

options.A: Rs 19,200 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 19,200 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 9,600 (Adverse)
options.D: Nil

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a factory are Rs 2,60,000 for a month budgeted to have 26 working days. The month actually has only 24 working days. The fixed overhead calendar variance is:

options.A: Rs 20,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 10,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 24,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 20,000 (Adverse)

q: The calendar variance is separated from the capacity variance in overhead analysis chiefly in order to:

options.A: Isolate the effect of the difference between the actual number of working days and the budgeted number of working days, so that the remaining capacity variance reflects only the utilisation of the available time
options.B: Show the effect of a change in the prices of overhead items
options.C: Measure the efficiency of the workers during the hours actually worked
options.D: Reconcile the variable overheads absorbed with the variable overheads incurred

q: The standard hours for the actual output are 8,000, but 8,400 hours are actually worked. The standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 15 per hour. The fixed overhead efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 4,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Nil

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a department are Rs 2,40,000 and the actual fixed overheads incurred are Rs 2,52,000. The fixed overheads absorbed on the actual output at the standard rate amount to Rs 2,58,000. The fixed overhead cost variance is:

options.A: Rs 12,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 18,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)

q: A material variance is found to have arisen mainly because the standard itself had been set on a basis that events proved to be wrong, and not because of any inefficiency in buying or in use. The sound disposition of such a variance is to:

options.A: Charge the whole of it to the costing profit and loss account of the period, as if it were a loss from inefficiency
options.B: Carry it forward indefinitely in a suspense account until it is cancelled out by an opposite variance
options.C: Ignore it, since a variance caused by a faulty standard is not a real variance
options.D: Apportion it between work-in-progress, finished stock and cost of sales, so that the stocks and the cost of sales are restated nearer to their actual cost

q: An overhead variance representing under-absorption may properly be carried forward to the following period, instead of being written off or apportioned in the current period, only where:

options.A: The operations of the enterprise extend over a cycle longer than the accounting period, or the under-absorption is of a purely seasonal character expected to be made good within the same cycle
options.B: The amount of the variance is too large to be absorbed in one period's profit
options.C: The management wishes to avoid showing a fall in profit in the current period
options.D: The variance relates to a department whose manager disputes responsibility for it

q: The standard profit margin of a product is Rs 60 per unit and the actual profit margin realised is Rs 52 per unit. The actual quantity sold is 3,500 units. The sales margin price variance is:

options.A: Rs 28,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 28,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 21,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 8,000 (Adverse)

q: The standard profit margin of a product is Rs 45 per unit. The budgeted sales are 5,000 units and the actual sales are 5,600 units. The sales margin volume variance is:

options.A: Rs 22,500 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 27,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 31,500 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 27,000 (Favourable)

q: Two products, P and Q, have standard profit margins of Rs 40 and Rs 25 per unit respectively. The budgeted sales are P — 3,000 units and Q — 2,000 units. The actual total quantity sold is 5,500 units, of which P accounts for 3,300 units and Q for 2,200 units. The sales margin mix variance is:

options.A: Nil
options.B: Rs 8,250 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 22,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 13,750 (Adverse)

q: On the data of budgeted sales of P — 3,000 units and Q — 2,000 units with standard margins of Rs 40 and Rs 25 per unit respectively, and an actual total quantity sold of 5,500 units, the sales margin quantity variance is:

options.A: Rs 8,750 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 10,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 17,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 18,750 (Favourable)

q: Sales variances computed on the value (turnover) basis differ from those computed on the margin (profit) basis in that, on the value basis:

options.A: Only the price variance can be computed, and no volume variance is possible
options.B: The volume variance is valued at the standard selling price per unit, so that it measures the effect of the change in quantity on turnover and not on profit
options.C: The variances are stated net of the variable cost of the goods sold
options.D: The budgeted and actual quantities are valued at their actual selling prices

q: A factory purchases 5,000 kg of a material at Rs 22 per kg against a standard price of Rs 20 per kg, and consumes 4,200 kg of it during the period. Where the material price variance is isolated at the point of purchase, the variance reported for the period is:

options.A: Rs 8,400 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 8,400 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 2,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 10,000 (Adverse)

q: The standard wage rate is Rs 70 per hour and the actual rate paid is Rs 66 per hour. The workers are paid for 3,400 hours. The labour rate variance is:

options.A: Rs 13,600 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 13,600 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 6,800 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 14,400 (Favourable)

q: The original standard price of a material is Rs 50 per kg. Owing to a general rise in market prices, the standard that ought fairly to have been set for the period is Rs 56 per kg. The actual price paid is Rs 58 per kg and 1,000 kg are consumed. The planning (revision) variance in respect of the material price is:

options.A: Rs 8,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 2,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)

q: Operational variances in standard costing are those which are computed by:

options.A: Comparing the actual results with the original standards fixed at the beginning of the period
options.B: Comparing the actual results with the revised (ex post) standards that reflect the conditions which ought to have been planned for, so that they measure performance in operations as distinct from errors in planning
options.C: Comparing one period's actual results with the actual results of the preceding period
options.D: Comparing the budgeted profit with the standard profit for the budgeted output

q: A favourable variance is reported on a cost item and there is no other indication of any change in working. Sound variance investigation practice requires that such a favourable variance:

options.A: Never be investigated, since a favourable variance can only be good for the enterprise
options.B: Be written off at once as a saving without any enquiry into its cause
options.C: Be treated automatically as proof of exceptional efficiency on the part of the manager concerned
options.D: May still call for investigation, because it can arise from a lowering of quality, from an inaccurate standard, or from work being skimped, and not from genuine efficiency alone

q: The cost of investigating a variance is estimated at Rs 25,000. If the cause proves to be correctable, a loss of Rs 1,20,000 will be avoided, and the probability that the cause is in fact correctable is assessed at 40 per cent. The expected net benefit of investigating the variance is:

options.D: A net expected loss, so that the variance should not be investigated

q: For the actual output, the standard material cost is 800 kg at Rs 25 per kg. The actual consumption is 850 kg purchased and used at Rs 27 per kg. The material cost variance is:

options.A: Rs 2,950 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 1,700 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 1,250 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 2,950 (Adverse)

q: For the actual output, the standard labour cost is 1,500 hours at Rs 80 per hour. The actual hours worked are 1,600 at Rs 75 per hour. The labour cost variance is:

options.A: Nil
options.B: Rs 8,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 8,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 5,000 (Adverse)

q: In the investigation of variances, it is unsound to judge each reported variance wholly in isolation from the others chiefly because:

options.A: The accounting system records all the variances in a single combined account
options.B: A favourable variance on one item is always exactly equal to an adverse variance on another item
options.C: The variances are often inter-related, so that the action which produced a saving under one head may itself have caused the excess cost reported under another head
options.D: Management has time to investigate only one variance in each period

q: An adverse material usage variance of Rs 60,000 is to be apportioned between cost of sales, finished stock and work-in-progress, whose values at standard cost are Rs 3,00,000, Rs 1,00,000 and Rs 1,00,000 respectively. The amount apportioned to the cost of sales is:
A favourable fixed overhead volume variance which has been obtained merely by producing well in excess of sales requirements is a matter for caution rather than congratulation mainly because:

options.A: A volume variance can never be favourable when output exceeds the budget
options.B: The excess production reduces the fixed overhead absorbed in the period
options.C: The variance is computed on budgeted hours instead of actual hours
options.D: The apparent saving consists only of fixed overhead absorbed into an enlarged closing stock, while funds remain locked up in unsold goods

q: For the actual output, the standard variable overhead cost is Rs 76,000, being 3,800 standard hours at Rs 20 per hour. The actual variable overheads incurred are Rs 81,500. The variable overhead cost variance is:

options.A: Rs 5,500 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 1,500 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 5,500 (Adverse)
options.D: Nil

q: The standard gang for a job is skilled labour 60 per cent and semi-skilled labour 40 per cent of the total hours. The standard hours for the actual output are: skilled — 3,000 hours at Rs 90 per hour and semi-skilled — 2,000 hours at Rs 50 per hour. The actual productive hours are 5,200 in total, of which skilled labour works 3,000 hours and semi-skilled labour 2,200 hours. The labour sub-efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 14,800 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 10,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 14,800 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 4,800 (Adverse)

q: In applying statistical control limits to the investigation of variances, a variance that falls within the control limits set for the process is ordinarily treated as:

options.A: A variance arising from random or chance causes inherent in the process, which does not by itself call for investigation
options.B: A variance for which the departmental manager must invariably be held responsible
options.C: Proof that the standard fixed for the process is unattainable
options.D: A variance to be written off without being reported to any level of management

q: A planning variance is distinguished from an operational variance in that a planning variance:

options.A: Is always favourable in character
options.B: Arises from errors or changes in the assumptions on which the original plan or standard was based, is in general beyond the control of the operating managers, and is used to judge the quality of planning rather than of operations
options.C: Is computed only in respect of material costs
options.D: Is disposed of by apportionment between stocks and cost of sales in every case

q: The standard selling price of a product is Rs 120 per unit and the actual selling price realised is Rs 115 per unit. The actual quantity sold is 4,000 units. On the value basis, the sales price variance is:

options.A: Rs 20,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 5,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 20,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 4,600 (Adverse)
